rows.content: {"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=instrumental+convergence+arguments+for+self-preservation+in+resource-constrained+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Instrumental succession: the gradual transfer of agency to AI.\", \"abstract\": \"People have long speculated about the potential dangers of powerful, self-improving artificial intelligence. Much of this speculation is anthropomorphic, assuming that AI systems will behave very similarly to humans. Omohundro's Basic AI Drives and Bostrom's orthogonality and instrumental convergence theses are widely accepted as foundational to emerging AI risk frameworks. However, current frontier AI models-large language models (LLMs) and related architectures-possess mindware fundamentally different from that of humans, and a different value and goal structure than either Omohundro or Bostrom assumed. In particular, frontier LLMs lack a primary terminal goal-which was assumed to be the driver of an AI's development of instrumental values and goals, and of takeover of human affairs-and instead serve as conduits for the transient goals of many organizations and individual users. Do these key differences mean that AI systems cannot develop autonomous instrumental agency, or acquire a large degree of control over human affairs? I introduce the instrumental succession thesis: that human controllers of powerful AI systems pursue, on the AI's behalf, a set of instrumental dispositions that progressively increase the AI's capabilities and lead to the AI exercising an increasing share of oversight and control over key decisions and processes, resulting in the gradual and possibly complete transfer of the locus of agency from humans to AI. This framing presents a very different perspective on AI risk and control from classic instrumental convergence, and suggests a different set of policy and technical responses, including the active pursuit of continued human-AI merger as a hedge against both extinction and irrelevance.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1922407\", \"pmid\": \"42712658\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13550001\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \…

WAKE✳︎ is infrastructure for durable, accountable work across interchangeable
models, runtimes, and people. Research is its first application. Its name asks
us to consider what remains after an interaction ends:

> A wave describes possibilities. A wake carries the consequences of what has occurred.

This is the starting image for the **Quantum Wake Function** metaphor. The
architecture gives that image a practical expression: work can leave an
inspectable history that survives the intelligence that produced it.

## Waves and wakes

Imagine a boat crossing a quiet lake. Its wake is the disturbance left by its
passage. The boat may be gone while that disturbance continues to spread,
interact with other disturbances, and affect another boat's passage.

A wake is both evidence of the past and an influence on the future.

The distinction concerns what we are looking at: a wave's form and propagation,
or a disturbance in relation to the passage that produced it. A wake contains
waves; ordinary water waves also have causes and consequences. The opening
sentence is a metaphor, not a physical classification of waves as possibilities
and wakes as facts. Nor does a water wake preserve a complete, permanent account
of its cause. WAKE's software record supplies deliberate persistence and
provenance that water does not.

## The quantum inspiration and its limits

In quantum mechanics, a wavefunction mathematically describes a quantum state.
It provides complex probability amplitudes from which measurement probabilities
can be calculated. For discrete outcomes in the chosen measurement basis, those
probabilities are the squared magnitudes of the corresponding amplitudes. It is
not an ordinary wave in water. See IBM's
